Beállítom Gulácsi Péter a Villarrealhoz igazolt, jelentette be a spanyol egyesület hétfőn. Az 58-szoros magyar válogatott kapus két szezonra írt alá a spanyol élvonalban szereplő csapatnál. Gulácsi 11 év után távozik az RB Leipzig csapatától, ahol 362 tétmeccsen lépett pályára. A Lipcsével 2017-ben és 2021-ben is második helyezést ért el a Bundesligában, 2020-ban az elődöntőig jutott a Bajnokok Ligájában, 2022-ben pedig az együttes az ő vezetésével hódította el története első Német Kupáját. A Transfermarkt szerint a spanyol csapat 2 millió eurós összeget fizetett a Lipcsének Gulácsi játékjogáért. A magyar kapust új csapata kedden mutatja majd be hivatalosan is a médiának. Marcel Schäfer, az RB Leipzig sportigazgatója a klub honlapjának arról beszélt, hogy Gulácsi „kétségkívül az egyik legfontosabb játékos” az egyesület történetében, aki „kulcsszerepet játszott a klub felemelkedésében”. https://nineoclock.ro/george-enescu-comp.text: ABOUT US NINE O’CLOCK STAFF 2024 COMMERCIAL OFFER – 2026 Subscribe to the Nine O’Clock 2026 CONTACT Special price offer 2026 with a 50% discount The 2026 George Enescu International Competition Begins: What Is New in the Anniversary Edition The George Enescu International Competition begins on Sunday, August 23, in Bucharest, bringing, at its 20th edition, one of the most significant transformations in its recent history. Until September 19, young musicians from around the world will compete in the cello, violin and piano sections in an edition built around the theme “In Pursuit of Excellence.” International masterclasses, a first-ever “play & conduct” semifinal format, career mentoring for prize winners, stage presence and well-being workshops, and an expanded programme reaching several Romanian cities are among the highlights of the 2026 edition. The anniversary edition brings, above all, a change of perspective: from competition towards development. For the young musicians arriving in Bucharest, the Competition becomes a space where performance, education, encounters with leading artists, stage experience and the first major career decisions are part of the same journey. The theme of the edition, “In Pursuit of Excellence,” starts from this very idea: excellence is seen as a continuous process in which discipline and virtuosity meet listening, communication and the ability to create music together with others. The model remains George Enescu himself — the complete musician, for whom performance, composition and a constant artistic quest were defining elements. International interest in the 2026 edition is confirmed by a record 819 applications from 58 countries for the Competition and its international masterclass programme. Following the pre-selection process, 150 young violinists, cellists and pianists have been invited to Bucharest to take part in the live stages. The total value of the prizes offered in the anniversary edition exceeds €150,000 . The programme begins with masterclasses in conducting, instrumental performance and composition, bringing young musicians into direct contact with internationally renowned artists and professors. The conducting and performance masterclasses are led by Cristian Măcelaru , Artistic Director of the George Enescu International Festival and Competition, while the composition masterclass brings together Zygmunt Krauze, Sarah Kirkland Snider and Steven Mackey , under the coordination of Dan Dediu . The conducting masterclass will conclude on August 28 with a concert featuring the participants alongside the Romanian Youth Orchestra . One of the major innovations of this edition comes in the semifinals. For the first time in the history of the Enescu Competition, the six semifinalists in each instrumental section will take part in a “play & conduct” experience with the Radio Chamber Orchestra . The contestant will simultaneously act as soloist and artistic leader of the ensemble, without a conductor. Beyond virtuosity, the challenge is designed to assess the ability to listen, communicate, inspire and build music together with others. The semifinals will take place at the Romanian Athenaeum on September 5 for cello, September 11 for violin and September 17 for piano. George Enescu’s music will also occupy a central place in the semifinals, with each of the three sections including works by the Romanian composer. For contestants arriving from around the world, participation in the Competition thus becomes an in-depth encounter with the music of the artist whose name the competition bears. The opening concert on August 23 at the Romanian Athenaeum, conducted by Cristian Măcelaru with the National Radio Orchestra , will bring back to the stage the prize winners of the 2024 edition — Mayumi Kanagawa, Yo Kitamura and Roman Lopatynskyi . The programme includes the world premiere of The Stone and the Ivy by Diego Santamaria , winner of the Originality Prize at the 2024 George Enescu Competition, Brahmsodia – Triple Concerto by Dan Dediu , and George Enescu’s Symphony No. 1 . Continuity between generations runs throughout the entire edition. Six chamber music recitals, six symphonic concerts and meetings with members of the juries and invited artists will bring before the public, among others, Marin Alsop, Claudio Bohórquez, Péter Nagy, Mihaela Martin, Nemanja Radulović, Laure Favre-Kahn, Alissa Margulis, Jenny Hyeonjeong Lee, Alexei Volodin, Ștefan Cazacu, Marie-Ange Nguci and Nelson Goerner . The 2026 edition also develops its relationship with prize winners after the competition ends. Philharmonic orchestras in Romania will include them in their upcoming seasons, while ARTEXIM’s institutional partnerships will open new opportunities for them to perform on European stages. For the first time, prize winners will benefit from a one-year career mentoring programme , developed together with Andreas Vierziger , focusing on repertoire, artistic decisions, relationships with institutions and artistic management, as well as the development of a professional identity. The programme also includes support tools addressing the artist beyond musical preparation: the “The Art of Presence” workshop, led by Valentina Băințan , and well-being sessions with psychologist Angelica Postu , focusing on managing emotions, stress and competitive pressure. A significant part of the Competition can be followed free of charge, including the stages hosted by the National University of Music Bucharest , masterclass activities at Sala Radio , and the first part of the semifinals at the Romanian Athenaeum dedicated to George Enescu’s music. For the first time, the Competition is also developing a dedicated network of inclusion partners, while expanding its presence across Romania. Sibiu, Constanța and Brăila will host recitals, masterclasses and concerts under the umbrella of the Enescu Competition. The 20th anniversary edition thus presents a Competition that looks beyond the podium — towards the developing artist, the professional community around them and the journey that begins after the competition. The 2026 George Enescu International Competition takes place from August 23 to September 19 in Bucharest, continuing a tradition that began in 1958 . The George Enescu International Competition is held under the High Patronage of the President of Romania. Photograph: Isar Aerospace/Franziska Kegel/Reuters View image in fullscreen The uncrewed Spectrum rocket successfully entered orbit after its launch from Arctic Norway. Photograph: Isar Aerospace/Franziska Kegel/Reuters Aerospace industry German startup sends first commercial rocket into space from Europe Isar Aerospace plans rapid expansion amid race to capitalise on expanding satellite-launch market Reuters in Oslo Sun 6 Sep 2026 09.21 EDT Last modified on Sun 6 Sep 2026 10.44 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A German startup has launched the first commercial rocket to reach orbit from continental Europe , a milestone for Europe’s efforts to secure independent access to space. Isar Aerospace said on Sunday that it would rapidly ⁠expand satellite deployments after the ⁠first orbital launch of ​its uncrewed Spectrum rocket from Arctic Norway , marking a ⁠breakthrough for a region where several countries are seeking a foothold in the fast-growing market for satellite launches. “Launch capability is right now the biggest bottleneck in the entire industry,” Isar’s co-founder and chief executive, Daniel Metzler, told reporters. Friedrich Merz, the German chancellor, hailed Saturday’s launch in a ​statement, calling it “the beginning of a new era”. Merz visited Isar’s ‌launch site in March, underscoring Europe’s ‌efforts to establish greater autonomy as the global order once championed by the US is shifting under the administration of country’s president, Donald Trump. The EU defence and space commissioner, Andrius Kubilius, wrote on the social media platform X: “Europe’s independent access to space just got a major boost.” Blasting off from Andøya Spaceport, Spectrum carried five small satellites along with an in-flight technology experiment. It was Isar’s second launch, 18 months after the company’s first rocket plunged into the sea and exploded in a fiery spectacle shortly after takeoff from the same site. Isar has said it already has five more rockets in production and is now focused on scaling up operations to meet rising demand, with a long-term goal of conducting about 40 launches a year. The German company ​is developing a second launch site in Nova Scotia in eastern Canada. Global players ⁠in the satellite launch market include Elon Musk’s SpaceX, which launches from the US, and the French firm ArianeGroup, ​a joint venture between Airbus and Safran ​that uses a spaceport in French Guiana, South America. https://www.dw.com/en/african-leaders-he.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5NXG0 Ethiopia’s Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed, Uganda’s President Yoweri Museveni and Kenya’s President William Ruto made a symbolic ceremony dig to celebrate the project Image: Luis Tato/AFP Advertisement African leaders on Wednesday broke ground on a new $16 billion (€14 billion) oil refinery off Kenya's coast. The project is expected to be completed in 40 months, and will process an estimated 700,000 barrels of oil per day. The refinery will be constructed at the coastal town of Lamu. Kenya's President William Ruto, Ugandan President Yoweri Museveni, and Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed were among the leaders who attended an event to celebrate the project, the largest of its kind in East and Central Africa. The refinery "will strengthen regional energy security, reduce reliance on imports and bolster our foreign exchange," Ruto said on social media. "But this is more than a refinery. It is an integrated industrial complex featuring a 1,000MW power plant, plastic factory and the manufacturing of fertilizers and chemicals." Africa's richest man, Nigerian industrialist Aliko Dangote , will oversee the project. Dangote: Project will reduce refined fuel imports, foster self-sufficiency Dangote said the refinery will make East Africa more "self-sufficient" by reducing imports of refined fuel. "For too long, our continent has actually been rich in resources but poor in value creation and addition. We have exported crude oil and imported refined products," Dangote said in his speech. "Such practice only leads to us exporting our jobs and opportunities that should remain on the continent and lead us into importing poverty into our nations. Africa cannot build lasting prospertiy by exporting what it has and importing what it needs," he continued. Nigerian billionaire Aliko Dangote (right) inspected earthmoving machinery with Kenyan President William Ruto (left) Image: Monicah Mwangi/REUTERS Lamu project faces environmental concerns, legal challenge The project, however, has faced resistance from environmental campaigners who fear it could harm Lamu Old Town, a UNESCO World Heritage Site which also hosts a fragile and unique marine ecosystem. The Lamu marine environment is also home to animals such as dugongs, whales and various sea turtle species. The Lamu region is home to an incredible variety of aquatic life [FILE: October 4, 2011] Image: Thomas Mukoya/REUTERS Lamu residents have brought a land rights legal case against the refinery, saying the site where it will be built is their ancestral heritage. Kenya's High Court on Monday ruled that legal proceedings will continue, but the groundbreaking ceremony can take place. Family and friends of murdered American nurse Mackenzie Michalski want the public to know the real "Kenzie" in a new article from The Irish Times . Mackenzie Michalski, a 31-year-old tourist from Portland, Oregon, was strangled to death by Dubliner Lorcan Murphy in his Budapest apartment on November 5, 2024. She had met Murphy, a former property developer turned internet marketing entrepreneur, in a nightclub before returning to his rented flat later that night. Murphy, who was later detained and questioned by police, confessed to the killing but claimed her death was an "accident" as a result of “consensual BDSM activity." In July, the 38-year-old from south Dublin was sentenced to 14 years in prison by a court in Hungary. Sign up to IrishCentral's newsletter to stay up-to-date with everything Irish! Two months after Murphy was convicted, the claims made at his trial remain fresh in the minds of Mackenzie's loved ones. “I knew in my heart that it wasn’t true,” Crystal Suarenzo, Mackenzie’s childhood friend, told The Irish Times. “Now, there’s some acceptance, knowing the evidence proved to the rest of the world that his story wasn’t even close to the truth.” Mackenzie "Kenzie" Michalski. (Photo: Facebook) At Murphy's sentencing, Mackenzie's mother, Jill Michalski, told the court how he “was allowed to tarnish our daughter’s reputation” and how her family had “suffered and will continue to suffer greatly” because of his “horrific actions." Mackenzie’s brother, Nicholas called Murphy’s conviction “a major step forward, but by no means the end,” referring to ongoing court appeals. “I don’t know whether I’ll feel any differently after the final judgment, but we’re not there yet. The fight for justice is far from over,” he told The Irish Times. Now, Mackenzie's loved ones wish to reclaim the public's image of her and challenge the narrative Murphy and his defense team attempted to tell in court. Known as "Kenzie" by her family and friends, they described her as “warm”, “bubbly”, “funny”, “quirky” and “passionate about life." Suarenzo described her friend as "freakishly smart, so brilliant – very, very capable but also so deeply silly." She told the Irish Times of Kenzie's love of animals, especially dachshunds, including Juniper, her pet dog at the time of her death. A native of Fredonia in New York state, Kenzie worked as a nurse in Buffalo, New York, for eight years, later specializing in neurocritical care. Diane Clark, her boss at Providence St Vincent Medical Centre in Portland, described her as "enthusiastic" and "passionate," but also a "professional" who was "calm and collected" under pressure. Kenzie was also a passionate traveler who had racked up dozens of country stamps in her passport from solo travels or trips with family or friends. “Wherever Kenzie went, she immersed herself in the local culture. She was never a casual tourist or vacationer,” said her brother Nicholas. In memory Fifteen months after her death, Kenzie's friends and family are still trying to cope with her absence. “Everything reminded me of her,” said Paula Prince, a close friend and St Vincent colleague. “I’d walk up the stairs and I’d see someone that I knew knew her, or I’d come around the corner and think I could just picture the two of us talking." Three candlelight vigils were held shortly after Kenzie’s death and three public celebrations of her life took place in Portland, Buffalo and Budapest. Read more Irish man charged with murder of American woman in Budapest Irishman disposed of US nurse’s body in suitcase in Hungarian woods Every month at Providence St Vincent Medical Centre, nurses participate in “Michalski neurosurgery rounds” – educational seminars on topics such as types of neurosurgeries or patient diagnoses – in her memory. Friends and colleagues also keep mementos or memorials to Kenzie in their homes and offices. Suarenzo often wears Kenzie’s birthstone (garnet) on a chain around her neck. “Anywhere I go, she’s with me." Kenzie’s loved ones were surprised at Murphy’s 14-year sentence, viewing it as too lenient. “To me, there was never going to be any amount of years that would have ever resembled anything close to justice,” said Suarenzo. Kenzie’s brother Nicholas described his grief as “beyond words." “Life without Kenzie is very empty and what’s left is very dark ... There’s no escape from the pain." Related: Crime , Dublin
